title: THEY TOLD YOU NOT TO QUESTION THE PREACHER. BUT WHY DID GOD GIVE YOU A BIBLE?
paragraphs: THEY TOLD YOU NOT TO QUESTION THE PREACHER. BUT WHY DID GOD GIVE YOU A BIBLE?

When searching the Scriptures becomes a threat to religious authority, we must ask a frightening question: Are we protecting the truth of Jesus Christ—or protecting something Jesus never told us to build?
There is a kind of fear that doesn't begin in darkness.
Sometimes, it begins in a church.
A believer sits quietly in a pew, listening to a sermon they have heard in different forms for years. The preacher speaks with confidence. The congregation nods. Everyone seems certain.
But something catches that believer's attention.
A verse is quoted. A conclusion is drawn. And somewhere deep inside, a question begins to form.
Is that really what the Bible says?
Not because the believer hates the pastor.
Not because they want to rebel.
Not because they have abandoned their faith.
But because they love Jesus enough to want to understand His Word.
So they go home.
They open their Bible.

They read the verse before the passage. Then the verse after it. They examine the chapter, compare translations, study the historical context, and begin to discover that the passage may not mean exactly what they were taught.
The next Sunday, they respectfully ask a question.
And suddenly, everything changes.
The warmth becomes tension.
The smile disappears.
The question is treated like an accusation.
And instead of receiving an explanation from Scripture, they hear something that leaves a wound:
"Who are you to question God's anointed?"
Now the believer is confused.
Because they weren't trying to challenge God.
They were trying to understand Him.
And that raises a question every Christian deserves to examine carefully:
Why would anyone entrusted with teaching God's Word feel threatened when God's people begin reading it for themselves?
Before we go further, something must be made absolutely clear.

Not every pastor who corrects a believer is controlling. Not every church that warns against a particular interpretation is hiding something. Not every independent Bible study produces sound doctrine.
Faithful shepherds have a biblical responsibility to protect people from error, and believers have a responsibility to remain teachable.
But there is an enormous difference between a shepherd who says, "Let's examine the Scriptures together," and a leader who says, "You must never question what I teach."
One invites you toward the truth.
The other may be demanding that you trust a human voice without testing it against God's Word.
And Scripture gives us a remarkable example of what faithful examination actually looks like.
In Acts 17, the apostle Paul preached in Berea.
Think about that for a moment.
This was Paul.
A man personally commissioned by the risen Christ.
A man whose teaching would become part of the New Testament.
If anyone could have demanded that people simply accept his message without examination, human reasoning might suggest it was him.
But look at what happened.
Acts 17:11 describes the Bereans as people who received the message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to determine whether Paul's teaching was true.
The Greek text contains an extraordinary expression:
ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφὰς καθ’ ἡμέραν
Anakrinontes tas graphas kath’ hēmeran.
Meaning, in context, "examining the Scriptures daily."
The verb ἀνακρίνω (anakrinō) carries the sense of investigating, examining, or carefully questioning a matter.
The Bereans weren't casually glancing at a verse to confirm what they already believed.
They were investigating the message against the Scriptures available to them, principally the sacred writings of Israel.
And here is the astonishing part.
Luke commended them for doing it.
They weren't condemned as rebellious.
They weren't shamed for asking questions.
They weren't accused of dishonoring Paul.
Their willingness to receive the message and examine it carefully was presented as something noble.
Do you understand what that means?
If examining the preaching of Paul was commendable, then examining the preaching of a modern pastor cannot automatically be sinful.
No minister today possesses authority greater than the apostolic message preserved in Scripture.
And no faithful minister should want people to believe an interpretation merely because of the personality, popularity, title, or reputation of the person delivering it.
But there is another side to this truth.
The Bereans didn't reject Paul's message simply because it challenged their previous understanding.
They received it with eagerness.
Their example wasn't arrogant skepticism.
It was humble discernment.
A teachable heart and a questioning mind are not enemies. In Christ, they can belong together.
And this is where the deeper problem begins.
Because sometimes what looks like a disagreement over Bible interpretation is actually a struggle over authority.
Imagine a church where every important decision depends on one person's interpretation.
The leader decides what a passage means.
The leader decides which questions are acceptable.
The leader decides which teachers may be heard.
The leader decides whether disagreement demonstrates spiritual immaturity.
Over time, the congregation may stop asking, "What does Scripture teach?"
Instead, they begin asking, "What will our leader allow us to believe?"
That shift can happen quietly.
Nobody announces it from the pulpit.
Nobody places a sign at the entrance saying, "Your conscience must surrender to our institution."
It happens through repeated warnings.
Through public embarrassment.
Through the suggestion that asking difficult questions proves disloyalty.
Through the fear of losing relationships, ministry opportunities, or belonging.
And for someone who has spent years loving their church family, that fear can be devastating.
Because sometimes the price of asking an honest question isn't merely an uncomfortable conversation.
Sometimes it is the loss of the only spiritual community they have ever known.
If you have experienced that kind of pain, please hear this carefully.
You do not have to choose between loving Jesus and asking whether a human interpretation of Scripture is correct.
But you also do not have to become bitter, isolated, or suspicious of every spiritual authority.
Jesus calls His people toward truth and love, not toward another form of bondage.
And His own ministry shows us why this distinction matters.
In Mark 7, Jesus confronted religious leaders who had elevated human tradition in ways that undermined God's commandments.
His words were severe.
Mark 7:8, in the King James Version, says:
"For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men..."
Notice what Jesus was confronting.
Not every tradition.
Not every religious custom.
Not every practice passed down through generations.
The issue was a human tradition being treated in a way that displaced obedience to God's command.
That distinction matters because traditions can help communities remember, worship, and learn.
But when a tradition is treated as untouchable even when Scripture exposes a problem, something has gone wrong.
The danger isn't tradition simply because it is old.
The danger is giving a human tradition authority that belongs to God.
And the same principle applies to modern churches.
A denomination can preserve valuable teaching.
A pastor can faithfully explain difficult passages.
A theological tradition can offer centuries of careful reflection.
A congregation can provide accountability that protects believers from serious errors.
These are not enemies of independent Bible study.
They can be its greatest allies.
But none of them is infallible merely because it has existed for generations, attracted thousands of followers, or earned the admiration of respected Christians.
Even sincere teachers can misunderstand a passage.
Even experienced pastors can make mistakes.
Even a congregation with beautiful worship and generous ministries can develop unhealthy habits around authority.
And even someone who studies the Bible independently can become dangerously mistaken.
That is why the answer is not to replace unquestioning trust in a pastor with unquestioning trust in ourselves.
The answer is to submit every interpretation—including our own—to God's Word, read faithfully in context, with humility and the help of the wider body of Christ.
The apostle Paul wrote in 1 Thessalonians 5:21:
"Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
πάντα δὲ δοκιμάζετε, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε
Panta de dokimazete, to kalon katechete.
In context, it calls believers to test or examine everything and hold firmly to what is good.
The verb δοκιμάζω (dokimazō) involves testing something to discern its genuineness or worth.
Paul was not telling believers to abandon discernment in the name of spiritual submission.
He was teaching them to exercise it.
But he was also not encouraging reckless accusations or contempt for spiritual leadership.
Just a few verses earlier, in 1 Thessalonians 5:12–13, he urged believers to recognize and esteem those who labor among them and admonish them in the Lord.
Both instructions belong in the same chapter.
Respect faithful leaders.
Test what is taught.
These are not contradictory commands.
They are part of a healthy Christian life.
And perhaps this is the balance many of us have forgotten.
Some believers have been taught to respect authority so completely that they fear examining a sermon.
Others have been hurt so deeply that they now reject every pastor, every church, and every form of correction.
Neither extreme reflects the whole counsel of Scripture.
Hebrews 13:17 teaches the importance of responding to faithful spiritual oversight.
First Peter 5:2–3 instructs elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not domineering over those entrusted to them, but becoming examples.
And 2 Corinthians 1:24 gives us an especially beautiful picture of apostolic ministry:
"Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand." (KJV)
Read that again.
"Not for that we have dominion over your faith..."
Paul understood something every spiritual leader needs to remember.
The people of God do not belong to the preacher.
They belong to Christ.
A pastor is not the Savior.
A denomination is not the Redeemer.
A ministry is not the Holy Spirit.
And no human being can occupy the throne that belongs to Jesus.
That does not make church leadership unnecessary.
Ephesians 4:11–16 describes Christ giving ministers to equip His people and build up His body toward maturity.
But notice the direction of that ministry.
Toward maturity in Christ.
Not permanent dependence on a personality.
Not fear of asking questions.
Not a congregation that knows its pastor's favorite sayings better than it knows the words of Jesus.
A faithful shepherd does not need to be the center of everyone's spiritual universe.
He knows who the center is.
And he wants the flock to know Him too.
Perhaps this is why some religious leaders genuinely welcome thoughtful Bible study while others respond defensively.
The reasons can differ.
Some fear that believers will encounter misleading teachings online.
And that concern is not imaginary.

The internet is filled with people who remove verses from context, distort Greek and Hebrew words, invent secret meanings, and promote themselves as the only teachers courageous enough to reveal the truth.
Independent Bible study is not automatically accurate simply because it is independent.
A person can read Scripture alone and misunderstand it badly.
Peter himself warned that some people distort difficult biblical writings (2 Peter 3:16).
James warned that teachers face stricter judgment (James 3:1).
Responsible leaders therefore have good reasons to care about how Scripture is interpreted.
But other leaders may struggle with pride, insecurity, institutional pressure, or the fear of losing influence.
A sincere question can feel like a personal attack when someone has confused their interpretation with their identity.
And in more troubling situations, a leader may use religious authority to discourage legitimate accountability.
We should be careful not to claim we can see every leader's hidden motives.
Only God knows the heart completely.
But we can examine behavior.
Does the leader explain difficult passages patiently?
Can a member ask a respectful question without humiliation?
Are mistakes acknowledged when demonstrated from Scripture?
Are members encouraged to read entire biblical books, not merely selected proof texts?
Is correction grounded in sound teaching, or does it depend mainly on threats and fear?
Does the ministry point people increasingly toward Jesus, or increasingly toward the unquestionable importance of its own leadership?
These questions matter.
Because spiritual authority is a responsibility to serve.
It is not a license to control.
And Jesus gave His disciples an unforgettable lesson about leadership.
In Mark 10:42–45, He contrasted rulers who dominate others with the pattern He expected among His followers.
Greatness in His kingdom would be expressed through service.
And then He pointed to Himself.
The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.
There it is.
The foundation.
The difference between worldly domination and Christlike leadership is not merely a management style.
It is the cross.
Jesus did not come to build a kingdom where frightened people would be forced to protect the reputation of religious celebrities.
He came to rescue sinners through His own sacrificial death.
He did not purchase His people with a pastor's influence.
He purchased them at the cost of His blood.
And that changes everything.
Because the ultimate danger of unhealthy religious control is not simply that people might misunderstand a doctrine.
It is that they may begin to experience Christianity as loyalty to an institution rather than reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
They may learn to perform obedience while hiding their doubts.
They may memorize religious language while quietly losing their joy.
They may become skilled at defending their church while struggling to explain the Gospel.
And then one day, when the leader disappoints them, their entire faith begins to collapse.
Not necessarily because Jesus failed them.
But because somewhere along the way, they were taught to place a human being in a position no human being was meant to occupy.
That is heartbreaking.
And if this is your story, I want you to know something.
The failures of a spiritual leader do not change the identity of Jesus Christ.
His resurrection does not depend on your pastor's integrity.
His grace does not disappear because a church treated you unjustly.
His Word does not become false because someone misused it.
And His invitation to come to Him remains open.
Matthew 11:28 records Jesus saying:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (KJV)
He did not say, "Come to Me only after you have satisfied every religious authority."
He did not say, "Come to Me only if you never ask a difficult question."
He called the weary to Himself.
But notice something equally important.
Jesus did not invite people into a life without discipleship, correction, obedience, or surrender.
He called them to take His yoke upon them and learn from Him.
Real freedom in Christ is not freedom from His lordship.
It is freedom to belong to the One whose lordship is perfectly righteous.
And that brings us to a truth that can be uncomfortable for both religious leaders and independent Bible students.
Sometimes the Bible challenges the preacher. Sometimes it challenges the person questioning the preacher. And sometimes it exposes pride in both.
The question is whether we are willing to surrender when Scripture corrects us.
Because the goal of Bible study is not to win arguments.
It is not to prove our denomination superior.
It is not to collect Greek words that make us sound intelligent.
It is not to embarrass a pastor.
It is not even to become the person in the room who knows the most verses.
The goal is to know God truthfully, understand His revelation faithfully, and respond to Jesus Christ in repentance, faith, love, and obedience.
Jesus warned in John 5:39–40 that people could search the Scriptures and still refuse to come to Him for life.
Imagine that.
Someone can study sacred words while resisting the Savior to whom those words testify.
That warning should humble every one of us.
The pastor who teaches.
The theologian who debates.
The independent student who investigates.
The person writing this article.
And the person reading it.
We can be correct about a biblical detail and still be cruel.
We can defend sound doctrine while neglecting mercy.
We can expose another person's error while refusing to confess our own sin.
We can become so passionate about discovering what is wrong with religious institutions that we forget to ask what Christ is correcting in our own hearts.
And if that happens, even our pursuit of truth can become another place for pride to hide.
So before you confront your pastor, examine your own spirit.
Are you seeking understanding or a public victory?
Have you read the passage in its literary and historical context?
Have you considered responsible interpretations that differ from yours?
Are you willing to be corrected?
Can you ask questions without assuming evil motives?
And if you are a pastor or ministry leader reading this, perhaps your questions should be equally searching.
Have you made it safe for sincere believers to ask difficult questions?
Have you ever used your position to silence someone you should have listened to?
Have you confused disagreement with dishonor?
Have you made your congregation afraid of examining your teaching?
Are you willing to say, "I was wrong"?
Because sometimes those four words reveal more spiritual maturity than a hundred sermons about humility.
And perhaps the most difficult question of all is this:
If someone discovers from Scripture that you have taught something incorrectly, would you rather protect your reputation—or help that person follow the truth?
That question is not only for pastors.
It is for parents.
Bible teachers.
Ministry founders.
Christian content creators.
And everyone who has ever influenced another person's understanding of God.
Truth does not become less true because we admit a mistake.
But our witness can become less trustworthy when we refuse to acknowledge one.
The Gospel gives us a reason to stop pretending we are infallible.
Because Christianity does not begin with the announcement that we are always right.
It begins with the devastating truth that we are sinners who need a Savior.
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." (KJV)
All.
The person in the pew.
The preacher behind the pulpit.
The scholar surrounded by books.
The believer who has just discovered that a cherished interpretation was mistaken.
And the religious leader who has wounded others through pride.
No one stands above the need for grace.
But Romans does not leave us there.
Romans 3:24 speaks of being justified freely by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
And Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That is the scandal at the heart of grace.
The holy Son of God gave Himself for people who could never save themselves.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed.
Not through the perfection of our theological knowledge.
Not through membership in the most impressive institution.
Not through our ability to defeat another Christian in debate.
But through Jesus Christ.
The One who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6).
And when the truth is a Person who loved us enough to die for us, pursuing truth should never become an excuse to stop loving people.
Perhaps you have been wounded by religious control.
Perhaps you were taught that questioning a sermon meant questioning God.
Perhaps you have carried guilt because you wanted to understand Scripture for yourself.
Or perhaps you are a leader who now recognizes that fear has shaped the way you respond to questions.
Wherever you find yourself, the invitation is not to hide.
It is to repent where repentance is needed, receive grace, and walk in the light.
A church can change.
A leader can repent.
A wounded believer can heal.
A broken relationship can sometimes be restored through truth, humility, accountability, and time.
And when restoration with a particular community is not possible or safe, a believer can still seek a healthy church where Christ is honored and Scripture is taught faithfully.
You do not need to abandon Christian fellowship in order to reject spiritual manipulation.
And you do not need to abandon discernment in order to honor faithful shepherds.
There is a better way.
A way where pastors teach with conviction and humility.
Where believers study with diligence and teachability.
Where questions are answered with patience.
Where correction is offered without cruelty.
Where the vulnerable are protected.
Where traditions are examined rather than automatically condemned or blindly defended.
Where the Scriptures are handled carefully.
Where no human personality is allowed to overshadow Jesus Christ.
And where everyone remembers that the Church has only one ultimate Head.
Christ Himself.
Colossians 1:18 says that He is the head of the body, the Church.
Not the most famous preacher.
Not the wealthiest ministry.
Not the oldest institution.
Not the most persuasive Bible commentator.
Jesus Christ.
So open your Bible.
Read slowly.
Pray for understanding.
Study the whole passage.
Learn from faithful teachers.
Listen to the wisdom of the Church across generations.
Test interpretations carefully.
Remain accountable.
Ask difficult questions respectfully.
And when God's Word exposes something in your own life, do not use someone else's failures to avoid your own repentance.
Because the most important question is not merely whether your pastor has been teaching the Bible correctly.
It is whether you are willing to obey Jesus when His Word confronts you.
Maybe you have been carrying a secret struggle.
Maybe your Bible has remained closed because religious disappointment made every verse painful.
Maybe you once loved studying Scripture, but someone made you feel that your curiosity was rebellion.
Or maybe you have been so consumed with exposing false teaching that your heart has become hard toward the very people Christ commands you to love.
Today can be a turning point.
Not because you have finally discovered every answer.
But because you can return to the One who is worthy of your trust.
You can say:

"Lord Jesus, forgive my pride. Heal what has been wounded. Give me discernment without arrogance, courage without cruelty, and humility without fear. Teach me to love Your truth more than my reputation, my traditions, or my desire to be right. Lead me into faithful obedience to Your Word. Amen."
And if that prayer reflects what is happening inside you, don't feel pressured to pretend you have everything figured out.
Sometimes the beginning of spiritual renewal is simply admitting that you need God's help.
Your testimony may help someone who has begun to believe that every church is unsafe or every spiritual leader is untrustworthy.
We need more than arguments in the comment section.
We need truth spoken in love.
We need repentance where harm has been done.
We need believers who are willing to listen.
And we need to remember that behind many theological disagreements are real human beings carrying real wounds.
Not to embarrass a pastor.
Not to attack a denomination.
Not to turn your friends against their churches.
Someone may need permission to open their Bible again.
Someone may need the courage to ask an honest question.
Someone may need to be reminded that Jesus has not abandoned them.
You may want to return to these passages the next time you encounter a difficult teaching or need to remember the biblical balance between discernment and respect.
If this message has helped you, I also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people move beyond religious performance into a growing, Scripture-grounded relationship with Jesus Christ.
We want believers to know what the Bible says, understand it responsibly, recognize error, grow in grace, and remain rooted in the Gospel.
And we want to keep making that kind of discipleship accessible.
These resources are part of our commitment to helping believers study, reflect, and grow—not merely depend on a short inspirational post.
But I want to be careful here, because the very message of this article demands integrity.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not a promise that money can purchase spiritual favor.
But partnership.
These products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
Our deepest desire is not to make you dependent on Gospel Warrior.
It is to encourage you to become increasingly grounded in Jesus Christ, faithfully connected to His people, and equipped to understand and obey His Word.
Because any Christian ministry that becomes more important than the Savior it proclaims has forgotten why it exists.
That includes ours.
The Gospel is too precious to be turned into a personality cult.
The Scriptures are too important to be used as weapons of intimidation.
And the souls of God's people are too valuable to be treated as possessions of religious institutions.
So if you have been afraid to open your Bible because of what someone might think, remember the Bereans.
If you have been tempted to reject every pastor because one wounded you, remember that Christ still gives shepherds to care for His people.
If you have been a leader who reacted defensively to honest questions, remember that repentance is not the end of your usefulness.
It may become the beginning of a more faithful ministry.
And if you have been searching for truth while carrying shame, confusion, anger, or spiritual exhaustion, remember the cross.
There, the perfect Son of God bore the judgment sinners deserved.
And through His resurrection, He opened the way to forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life for everyone who turns to Him in faith.
The Gospel does not promise that every religious institution will treat you fairly.
It promises something infinitely greater.
That Jesus Christ is sufficient to save.
That His grace reaches repentant sinners.
That His truth is worth pursuing.
And that His redeeming power is greater than the failures of those who claim to represent Him.
So don't let a human voice become louder than the Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep.
And don't let your disappointment with human leaders silence your willingness to hear His Word.
The most dangerous thing a church can lose is not its authority over people's questions—but its willingness to lead those questions back to Jesus.
